claims.claim: Criminal justice names the institutions and processes a society uses to respond to conduct its law defines as crime, conventionally grouped as police, courts, and corrections.
Criminology is the academic study of crime and delinquency - its measurement, causes, consequences, prevention, control, and treatment - rather than the operating institutions themselves.

BJS states that the United States apprehends, tries, and punishes offenders through 'a loose confederation of agencies at all levels of government' and that 'There is no single criminal justice system in this country.'
Criminologists were analyzing criminal punishment as operating in a 'loosely coupled system' by 1979.

Herbert L. Packer set out the crime control and due process models in 'Two Models of the Criminal Process,' 113 U. Pa. L. Rev. 1 (1964), carried into his 1968 book The Limits of the Criminal Sanction; he expressly said the models are not to be taken as describing real-world situations and that neither states what the process ought to be.
Packer pictured the crime control model as an assembly line or conveyor belt and the due process model as an obstacle course.

In the United States, very few crimes are under exclusive federal jurisdiction; police protection is primarily a function of cities and towns, corrections primarily a function of state governments, and most justice personnel are employed at the local level.
In June 2018 there were 17,541 state and local agencies performing law enforcement functions in the United States; local police departments accounted for 67% and sheriffs' offices for 17%.

At yearend 2023, 1,254,224 persons were under the jurisdiction of state or federal correctional authorities; 156,627 (about 12.5%) were under Federal Bureau of Prisons jurisdiction and 1,097,597 under state jurisdiction.
In fiscal year 2023, 94,411 suspects were arrested by federal law enforcement and booked by the U.S. Marshals Service, and U.S. attorneys prosecuted 61% of suspects in matters concluded that year.

BJS describes discretion as authority conferred by law to act according to an official's own considered judgment, exercised throughout the criminal justice system by police, prosecutors, judges, correctional officials, and paroling authorities, with limits that vary by jurisdiction.

In 2023 the National Crime Victimization Survey estimated that 44.7% of violent victimizations, 29.9% of property victimizations, and 42.7% of burglary or trespassing victimizations were reported to police.
BJS states that the justice system does not respond to most crime because so much crime is not discovered or reported to the police.

For 2023 the FBI released data on over 14 million criminal offenses submitted by more than 16,000 law enforcement agencies covering 94.3% of the population, so national police-based counts rest on voluntary agency reporting.

At yearend 2022, 5,496,400 adults were under correctional supervision in the United States, of whom 3,668,800 were on probation or parole and 1,827,600 were incarcerated, so most people under correctional control are not confined.

Federal sentencing law, 18 U.S.C. Sec. 3553(a)(2), directs courts to weigh just punishment, deterrence, protection of the public from further crimes by the defendant, and needed training or treatment - four distinct purposes in one statute, with restoration not among them.
Restitution to the victim is one of the sentencing options available in American criminal courts, which is the point of contact between the system's traditional purposes and restorative approaches.
The commonly reproduced flowchart of events in the criminal justice system updates the chart prepared by the President's Commission on Law Enforcement and Administration of Justice in 1967.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the American response to crime accurately called a 'system'?
positions: The word is standard in official usage: BJS publishes a flowchart of 'the sequence of events in the criminal justice system,' updating the 1967 President's Commission chart, and the term organizes textbooks, statutes, and agency budgets.

BJS itself describes the arrangement as 'a loose confederation of agencies at all levels of government' and states flatly that 'There is no single criminal justice system in this country. We have many similar systems that are individually unique.' Criminologists had described criminal punishment as operating in a 'loosely coupled system' by 1979 (Hagan, Hewitt & Alwin).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both, attributed, and treats 'system' as a useful label for a set of separately governed agencies rather than as a claim about coordination. It takes no position on whether the arrangement should be more coordinated.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What do Packer's two models describe?
positions: Classroom treatments sometimes present crime control and due process as descriptions of how particular agencies or political factions actually behave, including along conservative/liberal lines (as the SOU open textbook does).

Packer wrote that the models are normative constructions, that they are 'not to be taken as describing real-world situations,' and that neither is offered as corresponding to reality or as prescribing what the process ought to be.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows Packer's own framing: the models are ideal types for naming which values a practice favors. The political-alignment framing was not carried over, per the subject's requirement not to editorialize.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which purposes does the system serve?
positions: Retribution, deterrence, incapacitation, and rehabilitation appear together in federal sentencing law at 18 U.S.C. Sec. 3553(a)(2).
Restoration is a later addition associated with restorative justice and appears in American sentencing mainly through restitution, which BJS lists among sentencing options.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the five purposes as competing rather than agreed, notes that four are written into one federal statute while restoration entered by a different route, and evaluates none of them.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no verifiable content about criminal justice at all: it described the topic only as 'a foundational concept' students use 'to organize information, ask better questions, and explain relationships,' with a toolbox-drawer analogy and a map-legend analogy. None of it was sourced, and none of it was retained.

The draft's vocabulary list defined 'What Is Criminal Justice?' circularly as 'A foundational Criminal Justice & Criminology concept covered in this lesson,' plus three generic study-skills terms (context, evidence, application) that carry no subject content.
The draft's three questions tested generic study habits rather than criminal justice, and its 'worked example' described a student reading an unspecified scenario.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with sourced content; nothing of its wording survives.

Anchored every scale figure to a named BJS or FBI publication with its year: prison counts to Prisoners in 2023 (yearend 2023), reporting rates to Criminal Victimization, 2023, agency counts to the 2018 CSLLEA (June 2018), federal arrests to Federal Justice Statistics FY2023, correctional totals to yearend 2022. No total was asserted from memory.
Dated and attributed Packer to 1964 and quoted his own statement that the models do not describe real-world situations, rather than presenting them as descriptions of agency behavior.
Presented the system/non-system question with both positions attributed, using BJS's own 'loose confederation' language for the objection.
Stated U.S. jurisdiction explicitly, noted that state law and the limits of discretion vary by jurisdiction, gave no legal advice, and added an explicit educational-material statement.
Handed off component detail, the criminal/civil distinction, crime measurement methodology, and theories of causation to the topics that own them.
rightsIssues: No source in this packet is cleared for prose reuse. All government sources are recorded REFERENCE_ONLY and were used for facts only; the two short BJS quotations ('a loose confederation of agencies at all levels of government'; 'There is no single criminal justice system in this country') are attributed in the lesson text.

Packer's 1964 article is a copyrighted law review piece; one short attributed quotation is used and all other references are paraphrased. The full text was read from an Internet Archive capture of the Penn Law repository PDF rather than a paywalled host. The 1968 book is cited from its Crossref record only.
The SOU-CCJ230 chapter is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 at the chapter level (the book is CC BY-SA 4.0). Because of the NonCommercial term it was used for corroboration only, with no wording adapted.
Hagan, Hewitt & Alwin (1979) is paywalled; only the Crossref bibliographic record was verified, and the lesson's single reference to it is limited to what the article's title states.
18 U.S.C. Sec. 3553 is U.S. statutory text and is recorded PUBLIC_DOMAIN as an edict of government; it was read via the Cornell LII mirror.
The American Society of Criminology's self-description is copyrighted web copy; its content is paraphrased in the lesson, not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Justice System
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS), U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full page HTML directly (curl with a browser user-agent) on 2026-08-18. Supports: the description of the U.S. response to crime as 'a loose confederation of agencies at all levels of government'; 'There is no single criminal justice system in this country. We have many similar systems that are individually unique.'; the three-component sequence (entry, prosecution and pretrial, adjudication, sentencing, corrections); the statement that the justice system does not respond to most crime because much crime is not discovered or reported; the section 'Discretion is exercised throughout the criminal justice system' and its per-official table of discretionary decisions; the structural statements that very few crimes are under exclusive federal jurisdiction, police protection is primarily a function of cities and towns, corrections is primarily a function of state governments, and most justice personnel are employed at the local level; the sentencing options list including incarceration, probation, fines, and restitution; and the note that the flowchart updates the chart prepared by the President's Commission on Law Enforcement and Administration of Justice in 1967. No BJS wording was reproduced beyond two short attributed quotations.

sourceRecords.title: Two Models of the Criminal Process, 113 U. Pa. L. Rev. 1 (1964)
sourceRecords.provider: Herbert L. Packer / University of Pennsylvania Law Review
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record confirmed through the Crossref API (author Herbert L. Packer, University of Pennsylvania Law Review, vol. 113, iss. 1, p. 1, November 1964). sourceRecords.title: 18 U.S.C. Sec. 3553 - Imposition of a sentence
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, via Cornell Legal Information Institute
sourceRecords.license: U.S. federal statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the statutory text. Section 3553(a)(2) directs a federal sentencing court to consider the need for the sentence to provide just punishment, to afford adequate deterrence, to protect the public from further crimes of the defendant, and to provide the defendant with needed training, medical care, or other correctional treatment. Used as the primary-law anchor showing that retribution, deterrence, incapacitation, and rehabilitation sit side by side in one federal statute, and that restoration is not among them.

sourceRecords.title: About ASC
sourceRecords.notes: Read the page.
